title: The Straight Road
summary: Śānti sings of the straight road: those who take it, not swerving a hair's breadth from the royal road, win the eight great accomplishments and meet no toll station or guard post, while the fool, lost on an ocean of illusion and delusion with no boat or raft in sight, fails to ask the lord. The song ends by telling the listener to go the road with eyes closed. Munidatta reads the road as the path of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation and the lord as the true guru, and where the song closes the eyes, his yogi sees coupled union with eyes fixed and open (cp.15.m2, cp.15.m4, cp.15.m6).

lines.translit: saa sambeaṇa sarua biārem̐te alakkhalakkhaṇa na jāi
lines.gloss: self · awareness · true nature · in examining · mark of the unmarkable · not · goes
lines.en: On [examination]{vicara} of the [true nature]{svarupa} of [self-awareness]{svasamvedana}, the [mark of the unmarkable]{alaksya-laksana} does not go.

flags.note: na jāi, literally 'does not go'. (1) Kept literal: when self-awareness is examined, the mark of the unmarkable does not go, that is, is not reached. (2) jāi as a potential passive, 'cannot be (had, told)': the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mtshon du med, 'cannot be indicated'. (3) Munidatta makes Śānti the subject: he does not go into the examination of the mark of the unmarkable, which is conceptual thought (cp.15.m2). I kept the literal wording so as not to choose among them; 'cannot be reached' would read more easily.

biārem̐te is a locative of a participle or verbal noun, 'while examining, on examination'; the one who examines is not named. saa sambeaṇa sarua can be 'the true nature of self-awareness' (the thing examined, as I take it) or describe the examiner; Munidatta takes the true nature as Śānti's own, 'whose nature is the experience of self-awareness' (cp.15.m2).

lines.translit: je je ujūbāṭe gelā anābāṭā bhailā soī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: who · who · by the straight road · went · anābāṭā (off the road? no return?) · became · that one · [refrain cue, not translated]
lines.en: Whoever went by the [straight road]{ujubata} became [anābāṭā]{anabata}.

flags.note: anābāṭā is uncertain and kept in the source form per the glossary: (1) 'off the road, roadless', an- with bāṭa, answering ujūbāṭe; (2) 'without return', from anāvarta, the word Munidatta's paraphrase has in its place (cp.15.m2), which would regularly give anābāṭa; (3) the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'their road went elsewhere' (lam ni gzhan du song), as if āna, 'other'. See the note on this line.
Shastri prints the refrain cue ধ্রু after this couplet too, although the refrain is couplet 2. Not translated.

lines.translit: kulem̐ kula mā hoi re muṛhā ujūbāṭa saṃsārā
lines.gloss: by shore · shore · do not · be · O · fool · straight road · saṃsāra
lines.en: Do not go from [shore]{kula-shore} to [shore]{kula-shore}, [fool]{mudha}: the [straight road]{ujubata} lies through [saṃsāra]{samsara}.

flags.note: mā hoi re is 'do not be, O': literally 'do not be shore by shore'. I supply 'go' for readable English; 'do not keep to shore after shore' is also possible. kula could also be spelled for kula, 'family', but the ocean of couplet 3 favours the glossary's 'shore'.

ujūbāṭa saṃsārā has no verb. (1) Chosen: 'the straight road lies through saṃsāra', across or within it, in keeping with the crossing imagery of couplet 3. (2) 'Saṃsāra is the straight road', a siddha paradox. (3) The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) ends 'khor ba pa, 'one of saṃsāra', as if saṃsārā were a second address to the fool, 'worldling'. The final -ā may only lengthen the vowel for the rhyme with kaṇḍhārā.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) puts the sense of the first half in doubt: lus kyi ngo bo mi shes pa, 'not knowing the nature of the body', with no prohibition. It carries Munidatta's gloss of kula as 'body' (cp.15.m3) into the line.

lines.translit: bāla bhiṇa eku bāku ṇa bhulaha rājapatha kaṇḍhārā || dhru ||
lines.gloss: hair · split · one · bend · not · stray · royal road · kaṇḍhārā (golden? helmsman?) · [refrain cue, not translated]
lines.en: Do not stray one bend, a split hair's breadth, from the [royal road]{rajapatha}, [kaṇḍhārā]{kandhara}.

flags.note: bāla is taken as 'hair' (Sanskrit vāla) and bhiṇa as 'split' (bhinna), 'a split hair's breadth', as the Tibetan skra rtse, 'hair-tip', takes it; bāku as 'bend, crookedness' (vakra), which the Tibetan ma yo, 'do not swerve', supports. bāla also means 'child, novice', and Munidatta keeps addressing the novice yogin (bālayogin, cp.15.m3): a play on words is possible.
bhulaha can be 'stray, go wrong' (chosen, with the Tibetan log, 'turn aside') or 'forget': 'do not forget the royal road'. 'from' is supplied.

kaṇḍhārā is kept in the source form per the glossary. It may qualify the road ('golden', with the Tibetan gser lam and Munidatta's kanakapathadhārayā, cp.15.m3) or be an address ('helmsman', karṇadhāra). The comma leaves both open.

lines.gloss: of the ocean of illusion and delusion · end · not · you know · footing
lines.en: Of the [ocean of illusion and delusion]{mayamoha-samudra} you know neither the end nor the [footing]{thaha}.

flags.note: māāmoha may be 'illusion and delusion' (the glossary's rendering) or 'delusion about illusion', as the Tibetan sgyu ma la rmongs and Munidatta (attachment to māyā is delusion, cp.15.m4) take it.
thāhā is 'footing', a bottom within reach; the Tibetan has gting, 'depth, bottom'. 'Bottom' might read more naturally for an ocean.

lines.translit: age nāba na bhelā dīsaa bhanti na pucchasi nāhā || dhru ||
lines.gloss: ahead · boat · nor · raft · is seen · in confusion · not · you ask · lord · [refrain cue, not translated]
lines.en: Ahead no [boat]{boat} or [raft]{bhela} is seen; in your [confusion]{bhranti} you do not ask the [lord]{natha}.

flags.note: nāba na bhelā dīsaa: I take the single na as negating both, 'neither boat nor raft is seen', with the Tibetan (gru skyal rdzas mi mthong). 'A boat is seen ahead, not a raft' is grammatically possible but makes poor sense.

The second half is a plain statement in the Bengali. Munidatta (kiṃ ... na pṛcchasi, cp.15.m4) and the Tibetan (cis mi 'dri) both read 'why do you not ask?'. An unmarked question, 'in your confusion, will you not ask the lord?', is possible; I kept the statement. The Tibetan also makes the confusion what is asked about ('ask the lord about your confusion'), where Munidatta has bhrāntyā, 'in confusion'.

lines.translit: sunā pāntara uha na disai bhānti na bāsasi jānte
lines.gloss: empty · waste · that (the far end?) · not · is seen · confusion · not · you dwell (in) · while going
lines.en: In the empty waste the far end is not seen; do not dwell in [confusion]{bhranti} as you go.

flags.note: uha is uncertain. (1) Chosen: the demonstrative 'that, yonder' (compare Hindi uh), hence 'the far end'. (2) Sanskrit ūha, 'reckoning, inference'. (3) The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mtshan ma, 'sign, mark', and no negative: stong pa'i lam du mtshan ma mthong, 'on the empty road signs are seen', the reverse of the Bengali na disai.

na bāsasi is na with the present, not the prohibitive mā of 2a, so 'you do not dwell in confusion as you go' is possible as a statement about the one on the straight road. I read it as an admonition, like Munidatta's mā kariṣyasi (cp.15.m5). bāsasi is from bās-, 'dwell, feel, think'; the Tibetan reads it as vāsanā, 'latent tendency' (bag chags), and jānte as 'going' ('gro).

sunā is the adjective 'empty' (Sanskrit śūnya), the word behind doctrinal emptiness, which Munidatta reads here (cp.15.m5). The approved rendering 'emptiness' would turn the image into a doctrine, so I left 'empty' unmarked and listed the term in termsOmitted.
pāntara is Sanskrit prāntara, a long lonely stretch of road or an open waste; the Tibetan has lam, 'road'. 'Waste' avoids confusion with the glossary's 'road' (bāṭa).

lines.translit: eṣā aṭamahāsiddhi sijhae ujūbāṭa jāante || dhru ||
lines.gloss: these · eight great accomplishments · are accomplished · straight road · going · [refrain cue, not translated]
lines.en: These [eight great accomplishments]{astamahasiddhi} are won by going the [straight road]{ujubata}.

flags.note: eṣā is taken as 'these', agreeing with the feminine siddhi; the Tibetan 'di yis takes it as 'by this': 'by this, going the straight road, the eight great accomplishments are won'.

lines.translit: bāma dāhiṇa do bāṭā cchāṛī śānti bulatheu saṃkeliu
lines.gloss: left · right · two · roads · having left · Śānti · speaks (has spoken) · summing up (having gathered up)
lines.en: Leaving the two [roads]{road}, [left and right]{vama-daksina}, [Śānti]{p-santi} speaks, [summing up]{upasamhara}:

flags.note: bulatheu is taken as 'speaks, has spoken' (bol-, 'speak'), with the Tibetan smras and the convention of the bhaṇitā. Modern Bengali bul- means 'roam', which would give 'Śānti has roamed', fitting the roads. saṃkeliu looks like an absolutive, 'having gathered up', hence 'summing up' (Tibetan nyer sdud); Munidatta takes it as withdrawal, of the objects of existence (cp.15.m6).

lines.translit: ghāṭa na gumā khaṛa taṛi no hoi ākhi bujia bāṭa jāiu || dhru ||
lines.gloss: toll station · nor · guard post · grass (?) · thicket (?) · not · is · eyes · having closed · road · go · [refrain cue, not translated]
lines.en: There is no [toll station]{ghata}, no [guard post]{gulma}, no brush or thicket: with [eyes]{eye} closed, go the [road]{road}.

flags.note: The edition prints ghāṭanagumākhaṛataṛi as one word; I divide it ghāṭa na gumā khaṛa taṛi. ghāṭa and gumā are supported by Munidatta (ghaṭakuṭī, gulma) and the Tibetan (khral sa, sho gam). khaṛa taṛi is uncertain: khaṛa may be Bengali khaṛ, 'straw, dry grass', and Munidatta's list of hazards has grass, thorns, pits and hollows (cp.15.m6); taṛi I cannot identify, and the pair may be a jingle. The Tibetan line has 'gag, 'barrier', as a third item. 'Brush or thicket' is a guess.

ākhi bujia is 'having closed the eyes' (buj-, 'shut'). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mig gis shes pa'i lam, 'the road known by the eye', as if from bujh-, 'understand' (compare bujhasi, 3a). Munidatta has the yogi see coupled union with eyes fixed and open (cp.15.m6). I translate the song as it stands and do not harmonize.

jāiu is taken as an instruction, 'go', the content of Śānti's summing up. The -iu form may instead be an absolutive or a past, and Munidatta's paraphrase is in the third person (paśyati, 'he sees', cp.15.m6), which would give 'with eyes closed he goes the road'.

notes.text: Munidatta introduces the song as Śānti, delighted with full supreme joy, making plain the same meaning as before (cp.15.m1). Leaving out the refrain, he counts couplet 3 as the second verse, addressed to the novice yogin (cp.15.m4), couplet 4 as the third, on the greatness of the way (cp.15.m5), and couplet 5 as the fourth (cp.15.m6).

Rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. The heading names the melody to which the song is sung, Rāmakrī. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) calls it dga' bar byed pa, 'making joyful', as if the name were built from rāma, 'delight'.

The Bengali heading names only the rāga. The poet's name comes from the attribution śāntipādānām, 'of Śāntipāda', which the edition writes before the song (removed from line 1a as not part of the verse), and from the Tibetan heading, shAn+ti pa'i zhabs kyi'o, 'of Śāntipāda'.

Munidatta calls Śānti a siddhācārya whose own nature is the experience of self-awareness in the union of vajra and lotus, and says that he does not go into conceptual thought, the examination of the mark of the unmarkable and the like (alakṣyalakṣaṇādivicāraṃ vikalpaṃ na gacchati). He thus makes Śānti the subject of na jāi, 'does not go', and the examination its object; the line can also be read with the mark of the unmarkable as subject.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang rig rang bzhin rnam dpyod pa / mtshan nyid med la mtshon du med, 'examining the nature of self-awareness: it is without characteristics and cannot be indicated'. It seems to take alakkhalakkhaṇa as two negatives, 'without mark' and 'unmarkable', and na jāi as 'cannot (be indicated)'.

anābāṭā is kept in the source form because its sense is uncertain. It answers ujūbāṭe, 'by the straight road', and may mean 'off the road' or 'roadless' (an- with bāṭa, 'road'). The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de yi lam ni gzhan du song, 'their road went elsewhere', as if reading āna, 'other'. Munidatta's paraphrase has anāvarta, 'no return', in its place (cp.15.m2). In eastern Middle Indo-Aryan, Sanskrit -rt- regularly becomes -ṭṭ- and then -ṭ- (bāṭa, 'road', is itself usually traced to vartman), so anāvarta would also give anābāṭa: his word may be the Sanskrit of the song's word rather than a gloss, and the line may pun on both senses.

Munidatta reads the straight road as the excellent path of the avadhūtī of the joy of cessation: the lords of yogis of the past who went by it are fixed in the lotus grove of the wheel of great bliss, where there is no return. He quotes the Rativajra: this excellent path, the great rise of the Mahāyāna, is the one by which you will go and become tathāgatas.

Literally the fool is told not to be 'shore by shore' (kulem̐ kula), apparently going from one bank to the next instead of keeping to the straight way. The water imagery returns in couplet 3, with the ocean, the boat and the raft.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads lus kyi ngo bo mi shes pa / rmongs pa'i lam drang 'khor ba pa, roughly 'not knowing the nature of the body; the fool's straight road, one of saṃsāra'. It renders kula as 'body' (lus), the reading Munidatta gives in his comment (kule pratyekaśarīre, 'on the shore: in each individual body', cp.15.m3), adds 'not knowing the nature', and has no prohibition. Its 'khor ba pa may take saṃsārā as a second address to the fool.

Munidatta takes the shore as each individual body and the fool as the novice yogin (bālayogin), and says that apart from this path, the means of the joy of cessation, no other path leads toward the goal. He quotes the Rativajra: buddhahood comes by no other means.

kaṇḍhārā is kept in the source form because its sense is uncertain. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rgyal po yi ni gser lam, 'the king's golden road', and Munidatta's simile has a universal monarch entering his pleasure garden kanakapathadhārayā, 'keeping to the golden road' (cp.15.m3). Both seem to hear kanaka, 'gold', in kaṇ-, and Munidatta's -dhārā may echo -ḍhārā. It may instead be karṇadhāra, 'helmsman' (Bengali kāṇḍārī), as an address: 'the royal road, helmsman'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has skra rtse til 'bru gcig ma yo, 'do not swerve by a hair-tip or a single sesame seed'. It supports reading bāla as 'hair' and bāku as 'bend' (ma yo, 'not crooked'), but adds a sesame seed the Bengali lacks; its log, 'turn aside, go wrong', answers bhulaha.

Munidatta tells the novice yogin to form no concept to the left or right of the vajra path; his Sanskrit here (bāla vaṛe khādivikalpaṃ) is obscure, and the Tibetan comment has 'not even a concept the size of a hair-tip'. As a universal monarch enters his pleasure garden by the golden road, he says, so the lord of yogis playfully enters the lotus garden of the wheel of great bliss by the path of the avadhūtī. He adds a verse of Virūpākṣapāda on breaking the course of moon and sun so that the life-wind enters the avadhūtī.

Munidatta says that māyā is also called wisdom (prajñā), that attachment to it is delusion (moha), and that this attachment is the great ocean whose end, its measure, the novice yogin does not reach. He quotes the Anuttarasandhi: of all illusions the illusion of woman is the most distinguished, and in it the distinction of the three knowledges is clearly seen.

Munidatta says that on this ocean there is no means of crossing, such as a boat, apart from the true guru's raft (sadguruvāhyabhelaka; the Tibetan comment has 'by the true guru's word', as if reading vākya for vāhya). He takes the lord as the true guru (sadgurunātha), asks why the novice in his confusion does not ask him, and tells him to shake off confusion, take the means of the fourth joy from the guru's mouth, and so take the measure of the ocean.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has mngon du gru skyal rdzas mi mthong / 'khrul pa mgon la cis mi 'dri, 'ahead no boat or means of ferrying is seen; why do you not ask the protector about your confusion?'. It makes the confusion what is asked about and adds 'why' (cis), as Munidatta's paraphrase adds kiṃ (cp.15.m4); the Bengali has neither.

sunā is Sanskrit śūnya, 'empty', the same word as doctrinal emptiness. pāntara is Sanskrit prāntara, a long lonely stretch of road or an open waste without shade or houses. uha is uncertain: I take it as a demonstrative, 'that, yonder' (compare Hindi uh), and so 'the far end'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has stong pa'i lam du mtshan ma mthong / 'khrul pa'i bag chags kyis mi 'gro, 'on the empty road signs are seen; one does not go by the latent tendencies of confusion'. It has no negative where the Bengali has uha na disai, 'is not seen', and mtshan ma, 'sign, mark', for uha; it reads bāsasi as vāsanā, 'latent tendency' (bag chags), and jānte as 'going' ('gro).

Munidatta introduces this couplet as telling the greatness of the way, and warns the fool who has reached this path not, in confusion, to take clear light as 'empty' and so fall into annihilation (uccheda).

Munidatta says that right here, meditating on the self-blessing mind purified by clear light, one gains the eight accomplishments again. He quotes 'the scripture': having burned the lovely city of illusion with the fire of knowledge, yogis with the divine eye constantly see emptiness.

Munidatta says that Śānti the siddhācārya, having made it plain (sphuṭam) by avoiding the pair of appearances, left and right, made the withdrawal of the objects of existence (bhāvaviṣayopasaṃhāra). He thus takes saṃkeliu as withdrawal, where the line can also mean a summing up.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has lho byang gnyis kyi lam 'phrang spangs / shAn+tis nyer sdud gsal bar smras, 'abandoning the narrow ways of south and north, Śānti clearly spoke the summary'. Sanskrit dakṣiṇa means both 'right' and 'south', which may explain lho byang, 'south and north', for bāma dāhiṇa. Its gsal bar, 'clearly', has no word in the Bengali line but matches Munidatta's sphuṭam (cp.15.m6); its smras, 'spoke', supports reading bulatheu as 'speaks'.

The road has none of the posts where travellers were stopped and made to pay: the ghāṭa, a toll station at a landing or on a road, and the gumā, a guard or customs post. The last instruction is to go it with eyes closed.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has khral sa sho gam 'gag med pa'i / mig gis shes pa'i lam la 'gro, 'go on the road known by the eye, without tax place, customs post or barrier'. It reads bujia as 'knowing' (bujh-, as in bujhasi in 3a) rather than 'having closed', so that the eye knows the road instead of being shut; its 'gag, 'barrier', may answer khaṛataṛi.

Munidatta says that for one going by this path of the joy of cessation in the purified avadhūtī there is no fear of toll-house, guard post and the like, and no trouble from grass, thorns, pits and hollows. He then has the yogi see coupled union with eyes fixed and open (stabdhonmīlitalocane), where the song has the eyes closed; the Tibetan comment has them half-closed and unmoving (mig zim bu mi g.yo ba). He quotes a verse on the eyes, the bowed head and the stilled mind of those who gaze at emptiness. The divergence from the song is left standing.

termsOmitted.reason: sunā is the adjective 'empty' describing the waste; the approved noun 'emptiness' would replace the image with the doctrine. Rendered 'empty', unmarked; see the flag and questions.
Tibetan hit only: dga' ba is part of the Tibetan name of the melody (dga' bar byed pa, 'making joyful'); the Bengali heading has no word for joy.
Tibetan hit only: rmongs pa renders mūṛhā, 'fool', which is marked as mudha.
Tibetan hit only: gser lam, 'golden road', renders rājapatha kaṇḍhārā; the Bengali has no plain word for gold, and kaṇḍhārā is kept in source form (kandhara).
Tibetan hit (rgya mtsho); in the Bengali the ocean is part of the compound māāmohāsamudāre, marked as a whole as mayamoha-samudra.

questions: 1a: I kept na jāi literal, 'the mark of the unmarkable does not go'. Would you rather read jāi as a potential passive with the Tibetan (mtshon du med, 'cannot be indicated'), giving 'cannot be reached'? Munidatta instead makes Śānti the subject: he 'does not go into' the examination (cp.15.m2).

1b: anābāṭā is kept in the source form per the glossary. Since Munidatta's anāvarta, 'no return', would regularly give anābāṭa, and the word also plays on bāṭa, 'road', would you consider translating it ('roadless', 'beyond return') and putting the pun in the note?

2a: ujūbāṭa saṃsārā has no verb. I chose 'the straight road lies through saṃsāra'; the alternative is 'saṃsāra is the straight road'. Which do you prefer? I also supplied 'go' for mā hoi, literally 'do not be (shore by shore)'.

2b: kaṇḍhārā is kept in the source form. The Tibetan (gser lam) and Munidatta (kanakapathadhārayā) both point to 'golden'; 'helmsman' (karṇadhāra) is the other candidate. Should the line commit to 'the golden royal road'?

4a: sunā is the adjective 'empty'. I did not mark it with the emptiness entry, because the noun would turn the image into doctrine, and listed it in termsOmitted. Should the entry take 'empty' as a variant so the adjective can be linked?

4a: 'do not dwell in confusion as you go' treats na with the present as an admonition, as Munidatta does (mā kariṣyasi). As a statement it would describe the one on the straight road: 'you do not dwell in confusion as you go'. Please confirm. The uha reading ('the far end') is also a guess, and the Tibetan has no negative in this half-line.
3b: I kept the Bengali statement, 'in your confusion you do not ask the lord'. Munidatta and the Tibetan both have 'why do you not ask?'. Would you rather have it as a question?

5a: I used the source form [Śānti]{p-santi} in the bhaṇitā (keep-source) rather than the approved 'Śāntipāda', which I kept for the heading. Is that acceptable? I also read bulatheu as 'speaks' with the Tibetan smras, not as 'roams' (Bengali bul-).

5b: 'brush or thicket' for khaṛa taṛi is a guess (khaṛa perhaps 'straw, dry grass'; taṛi unidentified), and so is my division of ghāṭanagumākhaṛataṛi. I read jāiu as an instruction ('go the road'); Munidatta's paraphrase is third person ('he sees'). Do you have a preferred reading of either?

Commentary: Munidatta's bālayogin ('novice yogin', four times in this comment) is currently a form under the yogi entry, which would render it simply 'yogi'. Should it get its own entry before the weave?
